title: Exact string matching: naive scan vs Knuth-Morris-Pratt
problem_statement: Given a text T of length n and a non-empty pattern P of length m, count the positions i (0 <= i <= n - m) with T[i..i+m-1] = P; overlapping occurrences all count.

input.parameter: n = length of the text T. The pattern length m >= 1 is a second parameter: arbitrary in V1, m = n // 2 in the V2 scaling generator.
input.size_measure: n + m characters over a fixed alphabet. The scaling generator uses T = a^n and P = a^(m-1) b with m = n // 2, so m = Theta(n), the input has Theta(n) characters, and the naive worst case (n - m + 1) m ~ n^2 / 4 is Theta(n^2) as a function of n.

algorithms.name: naive matching
algorithms.idea: Try every alignment i of P against T and compare characters left to right until a mismatch or a full match.
algorithms.pseudocode: count = 0; for i in 0..n-m: j = 0; while j < m and T[i+j] = P[j]: j = j + 1; if j = m: count = count + 1; return count
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(max(n - m + 1, 0) m) character comparisons in the worst case (at most max(n - m + 1, 0) m, attained e.g. by T = a^n, P = a^(m-1) b), so Theta(n m) when m <= c n for a constant c < 1; Theta(n^2) for the m = n // 2 instances used in V2
algorithms.correctness: Exhaustive: each of the n - m + 1 alignments is checked character by character.

algorithms.name: Knuth-Morris-Pratt
algorithms.idea: Precompute the failure function (longest proper border of every prefix of P). On a mismatch, shift the pattern so that the longest border of the matched part stays aligned, so no text character is ever compared again after it has been matched.
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n + m) on every input: at most 3n comparisons in the scan and 3(m - 1) to build the failure table (this implementation compares the current character again in the if test after the while loop: per text character one if test and at most one failing while test, and every succeeding while test shrinks the matched length, which grows by at most 1 per character; the failure table is the same argument over the pattern). The bounds are tight up to lower-order terms: T = a^n, P = a^(m-1) b with m >= 3 and n >= m - 1 gives 3n - m and 3m - 6. Theta(n) when m = Theta(n)
algorithms.correctness: Knuth, Morris & Pratt 1977: after a mismatch following q matched characters, no alignment between the current one and the one keeping the longest border of P[0..q-1] can match. After a full match, continuing from the longest border of P finds overlapping occurrences.

shape.note: m = n // 2; for n <= 5 the pattern is degenerate and the count is irregular

relationship: The naive matcher re-reads up to m - 1 text characters after every mismatch, giving Theta(max(n - m + 1, 0) m) in the worst case, which is Theta(nm) when m <= c n for a constant c < 1. KMP never moves backwards in the text, giving Theta(n + m). With m = n // 2 (as in V2), or any m = Theta(n) with m <= c n for a constant c < 1, this is Theta(n^2) versus Theta(n).

sources.authors: Knuth, D. E.; Morris, J. H., Jr.; Pratt, V. R.
sources.title: Fast pattern matching in strings

sources.authors: Cormen, T. H.; Leiserson, C. E.; Rivest, R. L.; Stein, C.
sources.title: Introduction to Algorithms (3rd ed.)
sources.note: Section 32.1 (the naive string-matching algorithm) and 32.4 (the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm).

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree with each other and with an oracle that counts occurrences with str.find in a loop (a reference only) on random texts over {a, b} and {a, b, c} and periodic texts, n = 0..3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 50, 200 and 1000, with patterns that are substrings of the text, random short strings, or longer than the text; overlapping matches are frequent. V2 (since 2026-10-07, research/2026-10-07b_count_based_v2.md): on the worst case T = a^n, P = a^(n//2 - 1) b, the measured quantity is the exact number of CHARACTER COMPARISONS (== and !=) of the unchanged implementations. Characters of a str cannot be instrumented, so the scaling instance holds the same characters as tuples of an instrumented character type (CountingChar in harness.py); the implementations use only len(), indexing, iteration and ==/!= on characters, and on 200 random small (text, pattern) pairs plus the scaling instances they return the same answers on tuples as on strings. Naive: exactly (n - m + 1) m with m = n // 2 at n = 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200 (10100 ... 2561600); alpha = 0.998 against n^2. KMP: exactly 3n + 2m - 6 (failure function 3m - 6, scan 3n - m; valid for n >= 6, where m >= 3), i.e. 4n - 6 for even n and 4n - 7 for odd n, at n = 3000, 10000, 30000, 100000, 300000 (all even: 11994 ... 1199994); alpha = 1.000 against n. Tolerance 0.03: the counts are exact closed forms, so the band only covers lower-order terms (largest |alpha - 1| here 0.002, from the + n/2 term of the naive count) and stays below half the distance to the nearest rival. Rivals that must NOT fit, all rejected: naive against n (alpha = 1.997) and n^2 log n (0.928); KMP against n log n (0.910) and n^2 (0.500). The log factor is therefore resolved for both (validator diagnostic, RESEARCH_LOG RL-048). experiments/2026-10-07b_count_v2_apsp_strings.py reproduces every count above.

caveats: The naive bound is a worst case. On uniformly random text over an alphabet of size sigma >= 2 the naive matcher averages O(n) comparisons, since an alignment survives j comparisons with probability sigma^(-j). The V2 instances are chosen to be its worst case. Stating the costs as functions of n alone relies on m = n // 2 in the scaling generator; in general the worst-case comparison is Theta(max(n - m + 1, 0) m) versus Theta(n + m). KMP is optimal up to a constant factor for m <= n: on T = a^n with P = a, changing any unread text character would change the count, so every algorithm must read all n text characters.
notes: Related linear-time matchers: Boyer-Moore (sublinear on average), Rabin-Karp (randomized, expected linear), and the Z-algorithm.
